title: The do-while loop: run first, check after

visuals.title: Loop Lab: do-while runs once even when the condition is false

pairs.meaning: for loop: the count is known.

pairs.term: Read marks until the user types -1
pairs.meaning: while loop: the count is unknown and the body may run zero times.

pairs.term: Show a menu at least once
pairs.meaning: do-while loop: the menu must appear before any choice exists.

pairs.term: Ask for age again until it is between 1 and 120
pairs.meaning: do-while loop: ask first, then check the answer.

pairs.term: Sum of digits of a number
pairs.meaning: while loop: continue while digits are left.

stages.name: 1. Run the body
stages.detail: The body runs FIRST, with no check at all. So it always runs at least once.

stages.name: 2. Check the condition
stages.detail: Only now does the computer test the condition, using the values left by the body.

stages.name: 3. True: go back
stages.detail: If the condition is true, jump back to step 1 and run the body again.

stages.name: 4. False: leave
stages.detail: If it is false, the loop ends. Do not forget the semicolon after while (condition).

goal: After this you can write a do-while loop for menus and input validation, explain why it always runs at least once, and choose between for, while and do-while.
warmup: At a restaurant the waiter must bring you the menu before you can decide anything. He cannot first ask 'Have you decided?' because you have not seen the dishes yet. First he does the action (shows the menu), and after that he checks whether you want to order. An ATM works the same way: it asks for your PIN, and only after you type it can it check whether it is right. If it is wrong it asks again. 'Do first, check after' is a do-while loop.
definition: A do-while loop runs its body first and checks the condition after each round. Because of this the body always runs at least once. It is called a post-test (exit-controlled) loop. It is the only C++ loop that ends with a semicolon: do { ... } while (condition);
howItWorks: Compare it with while. In while the check is at the top, in do-while it is at the bottom. Run the pipeline: body, then condition. If the condition is true the loop goes around again, otherwise it ends. The classic proof: int i = 10; do { cout << i; } while (i < 5); prints 10 even though 10 < 5 is false, because the body ran once before the test. A while loop with the same condition would print nothing. Where do we use it? (1) Menus: show the menu, read the choice, repeat until the user selects Exit. (2) Input validation: ask for a value, and repeat the question while the value is invalid. Remember the semicolon after the final while (...). The bottom of the table below compares all three loops.

worked.problem: Show that a do-while body runs once even when the condition is false from the start.
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[i = 10]
  B --> C[/Print i/]
  C --> D[i = i + 1]
  D --> E{i <= 5?}
  E -->|Yes| C
  E -->|No| F[/Print final i/]
  F --> G([End])

sample.title: The body runs at least once
sample.expectedOutput:
Body ran with i = 10
Finished, i = 11

explanation.text: i starts at 10, which already breaks the condition i <= 5.
do: the body starts with no check.
Prints once. A while loop would have printed nothing.
Now the condition is tested: 11 <= 5 is false, so the loop ends. Note the semicolon.
Shows the final value of i.

steps.note: Enter the do block. No condition is checked yet.
The body runs once. Prints i = 10.
Now check: is 11 <= 5? False, so the loop ends after just one round.

worked.problem: Ask the user for an age between 1 and 120. Keep asking until the age is valid, then print it.
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Print prompt/]
  B --> C[/Read age/]
  C --> D{age < 1 or age > 120?}
  D -->|Yes, invalid| B
  D -->|No, valid| E[/Print age accepted/]
  E --> F([End])

sample.title: Input validation
sample.expectedOutput: Enter age (1-120): Enter age (1-120): Enter age (1-120): Age accepted: 21

explanation.text: The question is asked at least once, because no age exists yet to check.
Repeat while the age is invalid: below 1 OR above 120. With the typed values 150 and 0 the loop repeats, and 21 ends it.
Reached only with a valid age.

worked.problem: Menu program: show 1. Say Hello, 2. Say Bye, 3. Exit. Keep repeating until the user chooses 3. For any other number print Invalid choice. Trace it for the inputs 1, 5, 2, 3.
worked.flowchartMermaid:
flowchart TD
  A([Start]) --> B[/Show menu/]
  B --> C[/Read choice/]
  C --> D{choice = 1?}
  D -->|Yes| E[/Print Hello/]
  D -->|No| F{choice = 2?}
  F -->|Yes| G[/Print Bye/]
  F -->|No| H{choice != 3?}
  H -->|Yes| I[/Print Invalid/]
  E --> J{choice != 3?}
  G --> J
  I --> J
  H -->|No| J
  J -->|Yes| B
  J -->|No| K[/Print Program ended/]
  K --> L([End])

sample.title: Menu until Exit
sample.expectedOutput:
1. Say Hello  2. Say Bye  3. Exit: Hello!
1. Say Hello  2. Say Bye  3. Exit: Invalid choice
1. Say Hello  2. Say Bye  3. Exit: Bye!
1. Say Hello  2. Say Bye  3. Exit: Program ended.

explanation.text: The menu is printed before the user can choose, so we need do-while.
Any other number except 3 is invalid. Choice 3 prints nothing here.
The loop repeats until the choice is 3. Remember the semicolon.
Runs once, after the user has exited.

steps.note: First round: the menu is shown.
Check choice != 3: 1 != 3 is true, so go around again. Menu is shown.
5 is not 1, not 2, but it is not 3 either: Invalid choice.
Check 5 != 3: true, repeat. Menu is shown.
Check 2 != 3: true, repeat. Menu is shown.
No branch prints for 3. The check 3 != 3 is false, so the loop ends.

variations.when: Count is known. Checks BEFORE the body. Minimum runs: 0
Count unknown (sentinel, digits). Checks BEFORE the body. Minimum runs: 0
Must run at least once (menu, validation). Checks AFTER the body. Minimum runs: 1
for and while have no semicolon after the header; do-while has one after while(...)
Repeat the question while the answer is invalid

mistakes.error: No compiler error. The condition is reversed: it repeats while the age is VALID. The condition must describe the bad input.
No compiler error. i is never updated, so the loop is infinite.
No compiler error. A while loop checks first, so the menu never appears. Use do-while when the body must run once.
No compiler error. The extra second semicolon is just an empty statement. Harmless here, but it shows semicolon habits matter.

examTips: do-while always runs the body at least once. This is the number one exam point.
Write the semicolon after while (condition); at the end.
For validation the condition describes the INVALID input: while (age < 1 || age > 120).
Know the table: for/while check before, do-while checks after; minimum runs 0, 0, 1.
In a trace question write what is printed in every round, including the first round when the condition is already false.
romanSummary: do-while pehle body chalata hai phir condition check karta hai, is liye body kam az kam ek dafa zaroor chalti hai.
Menu aur input validation ke liye do-while best hai.
Aakhri while (condition) ke baad semicolon zaroor lagayein.
for aur while pehle check karte hain (minimum 0 runs), do-while baad mein check karta hai (minimum 1 run).
Validation mein condition ghalat input ko describe karti hai, jaise age < 1 || age > 120.

practice.prompt: What is the minimum number of times a do-while body runs?
practice.hint: The check is at the bottom.
practice.explanation: The body runs first and the condition is tested afterwards, so there is always at least one run.

practice.hint: The body runs once before any check.
practice.explanation: It prints 5, then i is 4 and 4 > 5 is false. The loop ends after one round.

practice.hint: Double x each round and stop when x is 50 or more.
practice.explanation: x is 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64. 32 < 50 is true so it doubles again to 64, and 64 < 50 is false.
b = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10. The loop stops when a becomes 5.

practice.prompt: Which loop is the best fit for a menu that must be shown at least once?
practice.hint: The menu must appear before the user can choose.
practice.explanation: do-while runs the body once before checking, so the menu always appears.

practice.hint: Look at the very end of the loop.
practice.explanation: A do-while must end with a semicolon after while (condition).

practice.hint: Keep repeating while the choice is not 0.
practice.explanation: The loop continues while choice != 0 and stops when the user types 0.

practice.prompt: Write a program that keeps asking for a number until the user enters a positive number (greater than 0), then prints it.
practice.hint: The condition describes the bad input.
practice.explanation: The prompt appears at least once and repeats while n <= 0.

quiz.prompt: When does a do-while loop check its condition?
quiz.explanation: The body runs first and the condition is tested at the end of each round.

quiz.prompt: What must follow while (condition) in a do-while loop?
quiz.hint: Look at the end of the syntax.

quiz.prompt: Which statement about the loops is correct?
options: Only do-while is guaranteed to run its body once
for always runs at least once
while always runs at least once
All three run at least once
quiz.answer: Only do-while is guaranteed to run its body once
quiz.explanation: for and while can run zero times. do-while runs at least once.

quiz.prompt: Which loop fits 'ask for a PIN again until it is correct'?
quiz.hint: You must ask at least once.
quiz.explanation: The PIN must be entered once before it can be checked, so do-while fits.

quiz.prompt: What is printed by int i = 7; do { cout << i; } while (i < 3);
quiz.hint: The body runs once before the check.
quiz.explanation: The body prints 7. The check 7 < 3 is false, so the loop ends.
